title: A hymn in Bihagra
hookLine: inside the Bihagra ballad, a salok headed with Mardana's name talks about wine

lines: A WINE JAR AND A CUP.
cards: A wine jar, a cup, and someone drinking far too much. Not the picture one might expect inside a holy book's night raga. But there it is, in the ballad of Bihagra in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Between the ballad's stanzas sit short verses called saloks, and some of them carry a heading with a name: Mardana, Guru Nanak's companion, the rabab player who traveled with him.

teach.h: THE DARK AGE IS THE WINE JAR.
teach.b: The ballad is the Var of Bihagra, with stanzas by Guru Ram Das and saloks set between them. One salok, headed Mardana, paints the scene, in plain English. This dark age is the wine jar.

teach.h: DESIRE THE WINE, THE MIND THE DRINKER.
teach.b: Desire is the wine. The mind is the one drinking. Anger is the cup, filled with attachment, and pride is the one pouring.

Anyone who's watched someone lose a night to drinking knows the picture: the cup keeps getting filled, and the drinker keeps reaching. The salok says the mind does the same with desire. Then it turns the picture around.
Make the body the still, it says, and from it draw a different drink, one that runs like nectar.

In the company of the holy, the cup becomes loving attention, filled with that nectar, and drinking it cuts the faults away. The night raga fits: the longing that might pour itself into the wrong cup is turned toward God.
Now, who wrote it? The heading names Mardana along with the mark the Granth uses for Guru Nanak, and Sikh readers take that in more than one way.
Some Sikh scholars read these saloks as Guru Nanak's own words, spoken to Mardana or about him. Others read the heading as giving the words to Mardana himself.
The Granth doesn't stop to settle it, and neither does this lesson.
Either way, a companion's name stands on the page beside the Guru's, in a ballad sung at night.
The longing doesn't vanish. It finds its proper cup.

how: The Var of Bihagra is sung in kirtan with its saloks, and Sikh scholars discuss the saloks headed with Mardana's name, reading them either as Guru Nanak's words addressed to Mardana or as Mardana's own.

games.q: what does “a hymn in bihagra” mean?
o: Mardana's salok: desire the wine, the mind the drinker
a hymn praising wine as a gift for celebrations
a drinking song sung at Punjabi village weddings

games.q: what's inside the salok — tap the pairs.

s: the Bihagra salok praises drinking wine
it uses wine as a picture of desire, then turns to a better cup, loving attention filled with nectar.
Mardana's name appears in headings in the Bihagra Var
a few saloks carry his name with the mark used for Guru Nanak.
everyone agrees who wrote the saloks headed Mardana
some read them as Guru Nanak's words to Mardana; others as Mardana's own.

games.q: a salok's heading names Mardana alongside the mark for Guru Nanak. who wrote it?
o: Sikh readers differ, and the text doesn't settle it.
games.why: both readings are held. the heading puts a companion's name on the page beside the Guru's, whichever way it's read.

practice: Think of the last thing you reached for late at night, scrolling, snacking, one more episode, one more glass, and just see the reach, without judgment.
Then ask what the reach was really for, rest, company, comfort, quiet, and hold that real wish for a moment. If you pray, offer it with Waheguru; if you don't, simply name the wish to yourself.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Bihagra. A salok in the Bihagra ballad, headed with Mardana's name, where desire is the wine and the mind the drinker, until loving attention becomes the cup and nectar the drink. Today's word.

orig.note: Mardana, Guru Nanak's companion and rabab player, named in salok headings in the Bihagra Var.

carryVoice: Your line: longing at night. Desire was the wine; loving attention becomes the cup. Until tomorrow.
